summary: Romania is located in Southeast Europe, with the Carpathian Mountains running through the country; it is the descendant of the Roman province of Dacia and is known for the castles of Transylvania and the legend of Dracula.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Christianity reached the lower Danube region in the Roman period, and the ancestors of the Romanians adopted Eastern Orthodoxy under Bulgarian and Byzantine influence and long held services in Slavonic. After the founding of the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia in the 14th century, Orthodoxy became the state religion. The Romanian Orthodox Church gained autocephalous status in 1885 and was raised to a patriarchate in 1925. During the communist period (1947–1989) the Church was controlled but not eliminated, and after 1989 Orthodoxy revived and many new churches were built, the People's Salvation Cathedral in Bucharest, consecrated in 2018, being a symbol of this.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholics are mainly the Hungarian and German minorities of Transylvania and the Csángós of Moldavia in the east. In addition, when the Habsburgs ruled Transylvania in 1700, some Romanian Orthodox believers united with Rome, forming the Greek Catholic Church, which promoted the Romanian national revival in the 19th century. In 1948 the communist government forcibly merged the Greek Catholic Church into the Orthodox Church, and it was restored only after 1989, by which time its followers had greatly declined.

ranking.name: Reformed Church
ranking.description: The Reformed (Calvinist) Church was introduced to Transylvania during the 16th-century Reformation, when the Principality of Transylvania was known for religious tolerance, and the Edict of Torda in 1568 recognized the legal status of several Protestant denominations. The Reformed Church is mainly followed by ethnic Hungarians, and so is concentrated in the Hungarian-populated counties of Transylvania such as Harghita, Covasna and Mureș.

ranking.name: Pentecostalism
ranking.description: Pentecostalism was introduced to Romania from the United States in the 1920s and was suppressed during the communist period, when believers were often monitored or even imprisoned. After 1989 Pentecostalism expanded rapidly, and Romania became one of the countries in Europe with the most Pentecostal believers, with particular appeal among the Roma and in rural areas.

religion.background: The territory of Romania came into contact with Christianity in the Roman period, and in the Middle Ages developed an Orthodox tradition under Byzantine influence. Transylvania was long ruled by Hungary and the Habsburgs, producing a pluralistic situation in which Catholicism, the Reformed Church and Lutheranism coexisted, and the Edict of Torda of 1568 pioneered religious tolerance in Europe. During the communist period religion was strictly controlled; after the revolution of 1989 Orthodoxy revived rapidly, and today Romania is one of the most religious countries in the European Union.

ranking.name: Romanian
ranking.description: Romanian belongs to the Romance family and descends from the vulgar Latin spoken by the inhabitants of Dacia after the Roman Empire conquered it in 106; it is the only Romance language in Eastern Europe and has absorbed a large amount of Slavic vocabulary. In the national revival movement of the 19th century, scholars stressed its Latin origin, and in the 1860s it switched from the Cyrillic alphabet to the Latin alphabet. After the unification of Romania in 1918 Romanian became the national language, and today more than ninety percent of the population speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Hungarian
ranking.description: Hungarian is the language of the ethnic Hungarians of Transylvania, who settled there in the Middle Ages with the expansion of the Kingdom of Hungary, and Transylvania was incorporated into Romania only in 1918. Ethnic Hungarians are concentrated in the Székely Land in the east (Harghita, Covasna), where there are Hungarian-language schools and media, and in places where ethnic Hungarians make up more than twenty percent, Hungarian may be used in local administration.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: Romani is the language of the Roma (Gypsies), which originated in northern India; the Roma arrived in Wallachia and Moldavia around the 14th century and were held as slaves for five hundred years, with slavery fully abolished only in 1856. Because of long discrimination and assimilation, many Roma have switched to speaking Romanian or Hungarian, so native Romani speakers make up only about 1%, while the actual Roma population share is higher.

language.history: Romanian descends from the vulgar Latin left by the Roman Empire in the region of Dacia, was influenced by Slavic in the Middle Ages and was written in the Cyrillic alphabet, with the Church using Slavonic in its liturgy. The earliest surviving Romanian-language document is Neacșu's Letter of 1521. In the 18th and 19th centuries the Transylvanian School stressed the Latin origin of the language, and in the 1860s the Latin alphabet was formally adopted. During the communist period the Soviet Union promoted 'Moldovan', written in the Cyrillic alphabet, in Moldova, and after 1989 the Latin alphabet was restored.

ranking.name: Sarmale (cabbage rolls)
ranking.description: Pickled sour cabbage leaves are wrapped around ground pork, rice and onion, placed in a clay pot and stewed for a long time with smoked meat and tomato, served with mămăligă and sour cream.
ranking.history: The method and name of sarmale come from the Ottoman 'sarma' (Turkish for 'wrapping'), and were introduced during Ottoman suzerainty over Wallachia and Moldavia in the 16th to 19th centuries. Romanians replaced grape leaves with pickled sour cabbage leaves and added pork. It is an essential dish at Christmas, New Year, weddings and Easter, and is regarded as Romania's national dish.

ranking.name: Mămăligă (cornmeal porridge)
ranking.description: Cornmeal is poured into boiling water and stirred constantly, cooked into a thick golden porridge that can be cut into pieces, often eaten with sour cream, sheep's cheese or stews.
ranking.history: Maize originated in the Americas, and after it reached Romania in the 17th century it quickly replaced millet as the farmers' staple grain, because of its high yield and suitability to the local climate. In the 19th century mămăligă was the daily food of poor peasants, and excessive dependence on maize even caused epidemics of pellagra. Today it is regarded as representative of traditional Romanian cuisine, remains the daily staple of farmhouses in mountain areas, and is the standard side dish for sarmale.

ranking.name: Mici (grilled sausages)
ranking.description: Ground beef, pork and lamb are mixed with garlic, thyme and baking soda, shaped into short casing-free cylinders and grilled over charcoal, eaten with mustard and beer.
ranking.history: There is a common legend about the origin of mici: at the end of the 19th century, when a restaurant in Bucharest ran out of sausage casings, the cook simply grilled the meat mixture without them, and so mici were born. The method is also thought to have been influenced by Ottoman and Balkan grilled meatballs. Mici are an essential food for Romanians' grill picnics on 1 May, Labour Day, and tens of millions are eaten across the country every year.

ranking.name: Cozonac
ranking.description: A fermented dough enriched with milk, butter, eggs and sugar is rolled around a filling of walnuts, cocoa, raisins or Turkish delight and baked into a large sweet loaf, which shows a beautiful spiral pattern when sliced.
ranking.history: Cozonac is a traditional dessert of Romanian Orthodox festivals, made in every household at Easter and Christmas, symbolizing abundance and family reunion. Making it takes hours of kneading and fermenting, and traditionally it is prepared by the women of the household before the festival. It also appears at Orthodox funerals and memorial services, as food distributed to guests.

ranking.name: Papanași
ranking.description: A dough kneaded from fresh cheese, flour and eggs is shaped into one large and one small round and deep-fried, the large one with a hole and the small one like a ball placed on top, drizzled with sour cream and berry jam.
ranking.history: Papanași are among Romania's most popular desserts; accounts of the name's origin vary, and the method is close to Central European cheese desserts, reflecting the culinary exchange between Transylvania and the Habsburg Empire. They use the fresh cheese common in rural Romania, are most often seen in mountain resorts and traditional restaurants, and are regarded by many Romanians as a dessert of childhood memories.
